title: Why do volcanoes erupt?
subtitle: Magma & plates
subject: sciences
description: A volcano is an opening in the earth's crust. Magma under pressure rises there and becomes lava. This is why the Earth “spits”.

hero.hook: Beneath our feet, the Earth is not frozen. Sometimes she opens a window of fire.

blocks.text: A volcano is not just a mountain that breathes fire. It is an opening in the outer envelope of the Earth. This way rises the **magma**: a mixture of molten rocks and gas under high pressure. Once in the open air, this magma becomes **washed**.
To understand an eruption, you have to look beneath the surface: the heat inside the planet, the movement of the plates, and the way the gases build up pressure, a bit like shaking a bottle of soda.

sections.title: Under our feet, nothing is still

blocks.text: The Earth is made of layers. On the surface, the **crust** is a rigid envelope, **5 to 70 km thick. Below lies the **mantle****, to about **2 900 km** depth. The coat is mostly solid, but over very long periods of time it can flow very slowly, like ultra-thick honey.

blocks.caption: An eruption: the rise of magma to the surface.

blocks.text: This internal heat causes matter to rise and fall: these are **convection currents**. They push out large pieces of crust called plaques. This is : the earth's surface is cut into plates which move apart, collide or slide against each other. [[Plate tectonics]]
Certain very rapid rises bring back diamonds formed at more than **150 km** depth. They don't have time to change on the way.

At , the plates move apart and the magma rises easily. In a zone of , one plate dives under another and carries water with it. This water lowers the melting point of rocks: magma forms, then rises. [[dorsal]] [[Subduction]]

Rock doesn't just melt "because it's hot." There are three triggers: a rise in temperature, a drop in pressure, or the addition of water. Once formed, magma is less dense than the rock around it. It therefore tries to rise, a bit like an air bubble in water.

Often, it stops first in a **magma chamber**, a reservoir a few kilometers below the surface. There, the dissolved gases form bubbles when the pressure decreases. If the “plug” of rock above no longer holds, the eruption begins.

The eruption of **Tambora** in **1815**, Indonesia, was so powerful that it cooled the global climate. **1816** was nicknamed "the year without summer", with disastrous harvests in Europe and North America.

Not all breakouts are the same. It all depends on the **viscosity** of the magma, that is to say whether it is rather liquid or sticky. A fluid magma, like at **Hawaii** or at Piton de la Fournaise (Reunion Island), lets the gases escape. Lava flows: eruption **effusive**.

A sticky magma traps the gases. The pressure builds, then everything explodes. Ashes, blocks and  (burning clouds of gas and ash rolling down the slopes) can then devastate the surrounding area. This is the style of volcanoes like Mount **Saint Helens** (United States) or **Pinatubo** (Philippines). [[fiery clouds]]

A volcano can also remain calm for centuries. In **79** after. BC, **Vesuvius**, near Naples, buried Pompeii under ashes. About **80%** of the world's volcanic activity happens beneath the oceans, far from our eyes.

Volcanoes shaped Earth's early atmosphere by emitting gases. Their ashes also enrich the soil: many fertile agricultural regions live at the foot of active volcanoes. But a very large eruption can send sulfur particles high into the atmosphere and cool the climate for months.

Some sites, such as in Yellowstone in the United States, are closely monitored. Under the sea, near the ridges, the [[supervolcano]] spew burning fluids rich in minerals. Ecosystems live there without sunlight, nourished by the chemistry of hot springs. [[black smokers]]
Volcanoes expel magma under pressure, especially at tectonic plate boundaries. The viscosity of the magma decides whether the eruption flows quietly or explodes.
